Market Sentiment

Phase 1 · domestic EOD evidence from validated local history

How to read the sentiment result Score not ready · run EOD update

The full score is not active yet. Load current EOD data to view the provisional domestic-market reading.

PositiveMost active evidence points to healthier market conditions. Treat this as supportive context, not an automatic buy signal.
MixedThe evidence disagrees or lacks breadth. Review the individual cards before changing portfolio risk.
NegativeMultiple inputs point to market stress. Review exposure and risk controls; this is not an automatic sell signal.

Reliability: fresher data, broader stock coverage and more available evidence clusters make the reading more useful. “Score not ready” means the six-cluster composite is still under development; the domestic reading is provisional.

Candidate v1 weights: cash trend 25% · participation and price strength 20% · volatility 15% · institutional flows 15% · currency and rates 10% · global risk 15%.

Candidate validation: Run the local analysis to evaluate evidence coverage. The candidate label and score remain hidden until validation is complete.

External historical-evidence readiness

External evidence enters validation only after enough dated observations exist and its directional thresholds pass a separate review. Sparse history is not treated as neutral.

How to read: Compare stored complete sessions with history required. Ready means the input has enough dated history for testing; it does not mean the input is predictive or that its candidate weight has been approved.
Evidence inputCandidate clusterWeightStored complete sessionsHistory requiredStored periodStatus
Run validation to audit external historical coverage.
Coverage readiness never activates a score by itself.
How to read: Each regime row summarizes what happened after that historical state. Median and positive/outperform rates describe typical direction; worst drawdowns describe tail risk. Give little weight to rows with small session samples, and compare excess returns only when a benchmark is selected.
RegimeSessions5d median20d median20d positive20d excess vs benchmark20d outperform rateWorst 20d relative drawdown60d medianWorst 20d drawdown
Run validation to inspect historical outcomes.

Transition-aware recovery review

Recovering market is assigned from prior regime history only: at least five confirmed weak/high-risk sessions followed by confirmed improvement. It lasts no more than 20 sessions and is evaluated only after the rule is assigned.

How to read: This table isolates sessions classified as recovering after stress. Compare the 20-session median and outperform rate with the worst drawdown: stronger typical returns with shallow tail loss are more stable, but sample size remains essential.
Transition stateSessions5d median20d median20d positive20d excess20d outperform rate60d medianWorst 20d drawdown
Transition-state results will appear with the validation report.
Recovery episodes and outcomes
How to read: One row is one distinct recovery episode. Entry and exit show duration and why the state ended; return, drawdown, and excess show the subsequent path. Episodes are historical examples, not independent trade recommendations.
Recovery entryPrior risk episodeExitExit reason20d return20d maximum drawdown20d excess
Recovery episodes will appear with the validation report.
This transition state remains validation-only and is not a current market signal.

Simple trend baseline

How to read: Use this simpler price-trend model as a reference point. If the more complex regime table does not improve typical returns, outperform rates, or drawdown behaviour versus this baseline, the added complexity has not earned its place.
Baseline stateSessions20d median20d positive20d excess20d outperform rate60d medianWorst 20d drawdown
The baseline will appear with the validation report.

Named stress-event review

Each event is compared with non-overlapping windows of the same length outside every named event. A high drawdown or stress percentile means the event was more severe than most ordinary historical windows.

How to read: Return and drawdown percentiles locate the event relative to ordinary control windows. Higher drawdown-severity or stress percentiles mean a more unusual adverse episode; recovery percentiles show whether recovery-state readings were also unusually frequent.
Review windowDatesIndex returnControl median returnReturn percentileExcess vs benchmarkMaximum drawdownDrawdown severity percentileRelative drawdownEntry regimeExit regimeWeak/high-risk sessionsStress percentileRecovering sessionsRecovery percentileFirst weak/high-risk reading
Named-event results will appear with the selected-index validation.
This is a risk-state test, not a direction forecast. A high-risk reading can be followed by a sharp rebound while still containing the worst drawdowns.

Month of year — NIFTY 50

Monthly return and trading-range summary.

How to read: Each row groups all observations for that calendar month. Count is the sample size; average return shows typical direction, average range shows movement within the month, and highest/lowest returns show extremes. A positive average is historical tendency, not a forecast.
PeriodCountAverage Return %Average RangeHighest ReturnLowest Return

Day of week

Daily-return behaviour grouped by exchange trading weekday.

How to read: Each row groups completed sessions by exchange weekday. Compare average return with the highest and lowest observations and check Count; a small average beside wide extremes usually indicates a weak, noisy weekday effect.
PeriodCountAverage Return %Average RangeHighest ReturnLowest Return

Turn of month

Last three and first three trading sessions of each month compared with all remaining sessions.

How to read: Compare Turn window with Other sessions. Average and median show effect size, while Positive Sessions shows consistency. The turn-of-month effect is more credible only when average and median agree and the held-out test below also survives.
WindowCountAverage Return %Median Return %Positive Sessions %

Held-out check — train vs. test

A validation frame intended to reject unstable patterns rather than certify predictions.

How to read: Train excess is discovered in the earlier sample; Test excess checks the later unseen sample. Same Direction is necessary but not sufficient. Survived requires the predefined consistency rules, and a failed row should not be presented as a seasonal edge.
PeriodTrain CountTrain Excess %Train SignificantTest CountTest Excess %Same DirectionSurvived
Load completed history to run the chronological train/test check.

Turn of month — held-out check

How to read: Compare the train and test rows separately. Edge is the turn-window daily average minus other sessions; the p-value measures how compatible the observed difference is with noise. Significant must remain true in both periods before treating the effect as stable evidence.
PeriodFromToEdge % / Dayp-valueSignificant
The edge is the turn-window average daily return minus the rest-of-month average daily return.

How to read these ratios

Sharpe measures return per unit of total volatility; Sortino focuses on downside variation. Beta measures NIFTY 50 sensitivity, while Jensen alpha estimates return beyond that beta exposure. Drawdown shows the largest peak-to-trough loss; Calmar compares annualized return with that drawdown.

The story contract

Identifier architecture

The system separates what was observable at the time from what happened afterwards. This prevents future outcomes from leaking into the historical label.

Layer 1

Point-in-time evidence

Store the prices, membership, macro releases and revisions actually known at each EOD.

Layer 2

Cycle identifier

Detect bull, bear, correction, speed, duration, trough and recovery without interpreting causes.

Layer 3

Regime fingerprint

Attach breadth, leadership, volatility, flows, rates, derivatives, earnings and macro states.

Layer 4

Behaviour hypotheses

Test observable proxies for optimism, crowding, fear, capitulation and recovery.

Layer 5

Outcome engine

Measure forward returns, drawdown, recovery, sector rotation and portfolio sensitivity on held-out periods.

Market-cycle taxonomy

How to read: A bullish or bearish phase needs a 20% reversal from a confirmed extreme. A correction is a completed 10–20% drawdown. A rapid bear is a research flag when the 20% decline is confirmed within 45 sessions; it is not an official “crash” declaration.

Bullish phases

Persistent advance from a trough, confirmed only after a 20% rise. We retain the earlier trough as the episode start without pretending it was identifiable in real time.

Bearish phases

Persistent decline from a peak, confirmed only after a 20% fall. Recovery is measured separately from the eventual trough.

Corrections

Drawdowns of at least 10% but less than 20%, measured from the prior running peak through trough and recovery.

Economic contractions: recessions and depressions

Equity-market cycles and economic cycles overlap imperfectly. The system will not call a recession or depression from price action alone.

Recessions

Macro history required

Planned evidence includes point-in-time real activity, employment, income, industrial production, credit conditions, inflation and policy. Release dates and later revisions must be preserved.

Depressions

Definition and macro history required

There is no universal mechanical depression threshold. We will freeze a severity-and-duration contract before publishing any episode, and will keep it separate from a bear-market label.

Behavioural fingerprints to test

Human emotion cannot be observed directly. These are measurable hypotheses we can compare across episodes before allowing them to influence the current classifier.

Optimism

Broad participation, persistent momentum, improving earnings and contained volatility.

Crowding

Narrow leadership, valuation dispersion, concentrated flows and one-sided derivatives positioning.

Fear

Breadth collapse, volatility acceleration, currency stress and defensive sector leadership.

Capitulation

Extreme downside breadth, forced-looking volume/OI changes, volatility spikes and rapid correlation convergence.

Recovery

Stress easing first, then breadth repair, improving leadership and confirmation from flows and earnings.

Backtest contract

A result appears here only after its rules, information set, universe, execution assumptions and validation split are frozen. Attractive charts cannot override a failed contract.

Step 1

Freeze the hypothesis

Specify the signal, eligible universe, rebalance timing, holding period and expected mechanism before examining outcomes.

Step 2

Rebuild the information set

Use only prices, membership, releases and revisions genuinely available at each historical decision date.

Step 3

Model implementation

Apply turnover, transaction costs, slippage, liquidity, delistings and unavailable-data rules consistently.

Step 4

Validate chronologically

Separate discovery, tuning and held-out periods; correct for repeated testing and compare with a relevant benchmark.

Step 5

Explain the result

Show return, drawdown, volatility, hit rate, turnover, regime dependence and the conditions under which the result failed.
